samples: Conard's editor's introduction defines film noir and neo-noir, cataloguing noir themes (moral ambivalence, alienation, pessimism, disorientation) across films like Blue Velvet, Angel Heart, L.A. Confidential, and The Usual Suspects, and previews the volume's thirteen essays. It argues neo-noir better embodies the noir outlook because its makers work self-consciously and can let criminals succeed. It closes by invoking Socrates' claim that the unexamined life is not worth living to justify philosophical reflection on these films.

Abrams argues that neo-noir differs from classic noir by replacing the search for an external villain in the city with the detective's search for his own divided self, structured through time (past, present, future noir). He reads Angel Heart and The Ninth Gate as theological past-noir, Blade Runner and Minority Report as high-tech future-noir where amnesia and precognition fracture identity, and Memento, The Bourne Identity, and Fight Club as present-noir where the sleuth must reconstruct himself from bodily clues; Leonard Shelby becomes a 'Sisyphus of memory' whose total self-consciousness recedes indefinitely.

Barad uses Blade Runner to test what distinguishes humans from machines. Against Turing's claim that indistinguishable input-output makes a computer a mind, she deploys Sartre's dictum that in humans existence precedes essence while manufactured replicants (like a designed android) have essence first, so they can blame their maker. She reads the Voigt-Kampff empathy test through Sartrean forlornness and despair, and argues Roy Batty achieves authentic humanity when he kills Tyrell and freely chooses to save Deckard, becoming a life-giver rather than his programmed combat model.

Smith reads Memento as a test of Locke's memory theory of personal identity. He explains Locke's view that consciousness of past actions (not soul or body) constitutes the self, rehearses Reid's transitivity objection and the circularity objection, and uses Parfit's account of memory and fusion to defend a survival-not-identity reading. He distinguishes 'Leonard 1' (anterograde amnesiac who returns each cycle) from 'Leonard 2b', a person fused from his own memories and those projected onto Sammy Jankis, arguing we too are 'fused' survivors who reinterpret hazy pasts, complicating responsibility and concern for our futures.

Spicer argues that the noir antihero embodies existentialism's darker side (alienation, contingency, dread), and that neo-noir intensifies this via European neo-modernism. In Point Blank, Boorman renders Walker's revenge as possibly a dying hallucination, using repetition, doubling, and drained color so that the story becomes an existentialist meditation on desire, faulty memory, and fragile identity. In Memento, Nolan's reverse-chronology 'Mobius strip' structure and Teddy's claim that memories are subjective interpretations leave Leonard's identity in tatters, ending both films on profound existential ambiguity.

Berger uses Harold Becker's The Onion Field to challenge Kant's moral idealism. Kant held that any rational being can deduce categorical imperatives and that conscience necessarily convicts the guilty and vindicates the innocent. Yet the killers Powell and Smith feel no guilt for murdering Kant-admiring cop Ian Campbell (Smith calls guilt a trick 'rich white guys dreamed up'), while the innocent, blameless Hettinger is destroyed by shame, thievery, and near-suicide. Berger weighs Schopenhauer's 'evil genius' objection and the sociopathy explanation, concluding Hettinger's guilt is a doomed attempt to preserve moral meaning.

book: 228 - The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film
essays: An Introduction to the Philosophy of Science Fiction Film
What Is It to Be Human Blade Runner and Dark City
Recalling the Self Personal Identity in Total Recall
Picturing Paranoia Interpreting Invasion of the Body Snatchers
Technology and Ethics in The Day the Earth Stood Still
Some Paradoxes of Time Travel in The Terminator and 12 Monkeys
Terminator-Fear and the Paradox of Fiction
The Dialectic of Enlightenment in Metropolis
Imagining the Future, Contemplating the Past The Screen Versions of 1984
The Matrix, the Cave, and the Cogito
samples: Sanders's editorial introduction surveys the twelve essays, arguing that science fiction film and philosophy are thematically interdependent, and previews each film's problem: Deckard's possible replicant status in Blade Runner, Biderman's existential reading of Quaid in Total Recall, his own paranoia interpretation of Invasion of the Body Snatchers, McMahon's Heideggerian being-toward-death in Frankenstein. He raises critical objections of his own, e.g. that the 'Deckard is an android' inference is logically invalid and that equating computer rationality with value-free computability (2001, Colossus) cannot yield normative judgment.

Knight and McKnight read Blade Runner and Dark City as noir-influenced cyberpunk that asks what it is to be human. They argue that Deckard's replicant status (the origami unicorn, the shared family photo) and Murdoch's serially reprogrammed memory show memory to be unreliable, invoking Locke's prince-and-cobbler thought experiment and the problem of new brains in one body. Their conclusion is that it is emotion and relationship, not memory, that ground agency and personhood: Roy's empathy in dying and Deckard's love for Rachael, Murdoch's love for Emma/Anna, are what mark the characters as human.

Biderman uses Quaid/Hauser in Total Recall to test criteria of personal identity: the body criterion fails on Kuato and George sharing a body, the brain and Lockean memory criteria fail on implanted false memories and memory gaps, and psychological continuity fails on how radically Quaid differs from the malicious Hauser. Facing Hume's conclusion that the self is a fiction (echoed by Wittgenstein and Derrida's deconstruction), he argues Quaid escapes it through the Sartrean existential route: thrown into existence, he takes a stance toward his facticity and, following Kuato's 'you are what you do,' authentically creates himself by rejecting Hauser and saving Mars.

Sanders rejects the standard Cold War-allegory and feminist readings of Invasion of the Body Snatchers and argues the film is best understood as film noir dramatizing paranoia. He shows that the mechanics of pod duplication are riddled with incoherence (multiple duplicates, location, timing, matching), then reads the frame story as evidence that Miles's whole account is a delusional psychosis. Dr. Hill's acceptance of the wild story on flimsy evidence violates Hume's maxim that a rational person proportions belief to evidence, making the film an ironic meditation on the philosophical significance of paranoia and lost humanity.

McMahon gives an existential reading of Whale's Frankenstein and Shelley's novel through Heidegger's being-toward-death and Ernest Becker's denial of death. Victor Frankenstein exemplifies Becker's 'defiant Promethianism,' the offensive denial that seeks to conquer death, and the monster personifies death itself. She argues his obsession erodes his humanity, estranges him from others, and generates moral dilemmas, illustrating Heidegger's claim that only authentic acceptance of mortality restores individuality and genuine community, so that mastering death would make us monsters.

Skoble reads The Day the Earth Stood Still as an allegory about the ethics of force and technology. He argues Klaatu's ultimatum extends Mill's harm principle to the interplanetary level: societies may fight among themselves but not threaten others, so Gort's robot police enforce a right to peace that no one has a right to violate. He distinguishes the robots' narrow, non-paternalistic authority from Hobbes's absolute sovereign, defends the ultimatum as preemptive self-defense rather than a rights violation, and contrasts the film's trust in machines with the later technophobia of Colossus and The Terminator.

essays: Not the Crime, but the Man Sherlock Holmes and Charles Augustus Milverton
A Case of Insincerity What does it Mean to Deceive Someone
Watsons, Adlers, Lestrades, and Moriarties On the Nature of Friends and Enemies
Eliminating the Impossible Sherlock Holmes and the Supernatural
Was it Morally Wrong to Kill Off Sherlock Holmes
Sherlock Holmes and the Ethics of Hyperspecialization
The Dog that did not Bark Learning how to Read “The Book of Life”
The Grim Reaper on Baker Street
samples: Baggett reconstructs Holmes's detective practice as an expansive epistemology built on observation, background knowledge, and abductive inference-to-the-best-explanation, using cases like 'The Blue Carbuncle' hat and the 'eliminate the impossible' maxim. He argues Holmes's boldness in drawing inferences is intellectual courage rather than hubris, invoking William James on the risk of losing truth by excessive caution. He then tests Holmes against feminist epistemologists who fault his cult of cold objectivity and mistrust of women (the Mary Morstan and Irene Adler episodes), concluding Holmes is partly vindicated by his imagination, intuition, and passion but still too fragmented between reason and emotion.

Rozema examines 'The Adventure of Charles Augustus Milverton,' in which Holmes burgles a blackmailer's house, feigns an engagement to the maid, and watches Milverton's murder without intervening. He argues that Kantian deontology (too abstract to judge rectification) and consequentialism (paralyzed by unpredictable outcomes) both fail to assess Holmes's acts, whereas Plato and Aristotle's virtue ethics fits: judging the man's character over the isolated act. Citing Plato's 'true falsehood' vs. 'falsehood in words' and Aristotle on voluntary acts and the storm-tossed captain jettisoning cargo, he concludes a virtuous person may rightly do what is normally forbidden against a vicious foe like Milverton.

Kinghorn builds a definition of deception by successively refining it against Holmes cases: honest error ('A Scandal in Bohemia'), double-bluffing ('The Empty House' wax bust), deceiving about a different proposition (the Windibank/'Hosmer Angel' interview), and non-deceptive manipulation (the drug-induced 'Creeping Man'). Invoking Wittgenstein on language as a public practice learned by trusting others' sincerity, he argues deception requires the target's mistaken reliance on someone's assumed sincerity. The surprising upshot: because Holmes and Moriarty mutually presume insincerity in their game, Holmes never truly deceives Moriarty.

Pigliucci shows that Holmes's celebrated 'deduction' is really a mix of induction and abduction, contrasting Aristotelian syllogism and Cartesian rationalism (with its failed Cartesian circle) against the fallibility of real investigation. He walks through Hume's problem of induction (Russell's inductivist chicken), the Mill-Whewell 'great induction debate,' and Popper's falsificationism—qualified by the Neptune/Uranus episode where scientists shielded Newton. Using 'Thor Bridge' and 'The Three Students,' he concludes Holmes is a pragmatic scientist wielding a whole toolbox, since there is no single scientific method.

Tallon applies Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics taxonomy of friendship—of use, of pleasure, and of virtue—to Holmes's relationships, plus Aquinas on friends helping each other flourish. The Baker Street Irregulars and Mrs. Hudson are friends of use; Holmes has few friends of pleasure; Watson is the friend of virtue, an 'other self' sharing virtue, support, and activity (getting Holmes off cocaine, taking a bullet). Inverting the account, he classifies Holmes's enemies as competitor (Irene Adler), rival/'frenemy' (Lestrade and Gregson), and foe (Moriarty), arguing a foe—an anti-self—can never become a friend.

Blanchette uses the Guy Ritchie film's Lord Blackwood 'resurrection' and 'The Hound of the Baskervilles' to ask whether a supernatural explanation is ever admissible. Drawing on Draper's definition of nature vs. the supernatural, Plantinga's natural-vs-logical necessity distinction, and Hume on miracles, he argues miracles are naturally impossible but not logically impossible unless nature is proven a closed system. He defends a truth-aimed methodology (pursue natural causes until the best explanation of failure is that none exists), showing Holmes rightly debunks both cases while thought experiments reveal conditions under which a supernatural verdict would become the rational inference.

essays: The Symbolism of Blood in Clockers
The Prostitution Trap of Elite Sport in He Got Game
Aristotle and MacIntyre on Justice in 25th Hour
We Can’t Get Off the Bus A Commentary on Spike Lee and Moral Motivation
Monsters and Moralism in Summer of Sam
(Still) Fighting the Power Public Space and the Unspeakable Privacy of the Other in Do the Right Thing
Coworking in the Kingdom of Culture Identity and Community in the Films of Spike Lee
Feminists and “Freaks” She’s Gotta Have It and Girl 6
The Dialectic of King and X in Do the Right Thing
Fevered Desires and Interracial Intimacies in Jungle Fever
Transcendence and Sublimity in Spike Lee’s Signature Shot
Rethinking the First Person Autobiography, Authorship, and the Contested Self in Malcolm X
samples: McFarland reads Lee's Clockers through Paul Ricoeur's account of defilement and Greek tragedy, arguing the film treats spilt blood as an 'unspeakable' evil that resists narrative and legal containment. He compares the ulcer-ridden, cleanliness-obsessed dealer Strike to Philoctetes and Oedipus, tracing how bloodstain passes through family lines (Rodney, Errol, Tyrone, Victor) and how detective Rocco's law fails to purge the contagion. The final train-into-the-desert shot leaves Strike, like an exiled tragic figure, neither cleansed nor at home.

Holt and Pitter argue that Lee's He Got Game exposes a 'prostitution trap' in which elite athletes, like literal prostitutes, become commodified bodies alienated from themselves. They read the parallel plots of star recruit Jesus Shuttlesworth, his father Jake pressured to broker a signing, and the prostitute Dakota as three versions of the same trap, invoking MacIntyre's internal-versus-external goods and Deci/Ryan's intrinsic-versus-extrinsic rewards to show how coercive money threatens Jesus's love of the game. Jesus escapes by exercising autonomy, negotiating on his own terms and skipping the press conference to reach an 'authentic realism.'

Conard uses Lee's 25th Hour to test Aristotle's claim that justice is inseparable from community and necessary for eudaimonia, and MacIntyre's charge that liberal individualist society lacks any common good. Comparing the greedy Wall Street broker Frank (an Aristotelian overreacher driven by pleonexia) with the drug dealer Monty (fairer, though convicted under unjust Rockefeller laws), he argues Monty is not unjust yet still cannot flourish in a fragmented New York. Monty's profane bathroom 'fuck you' soliloquy dramatizes the city's incommensurable values, while the post-9/11 fellow-feeling offers a fleeting glimpse of the shared good MacIntyre says modern society lacks.

Beckles-Raymond reads Lee's Get on the Bus to defend a communitarian 'encumbered self' against the liberal 'unencumbered self,' arguing the Million Man March riders' racial identity is inseparable from their moral motivation. Drawing on Charles Taylor's strong evaluations and critiquing Tommie Shelby's thin-blackness solidarity, she shows each rider (George, Evan Sr., Jay, Jeremiah, Jamal, Xavier, Gary, Kyle, Randall) attends because being a good man is bound to being black, while the ejection of the self-hating Wendell marks the limits of thin identity. The film argues raced persons 'cannot get off the bus.'

Palmer argues Lee's Summer of Sam is less ethnography than moralism about the diffuse 'evil energy' that spreads through an Italian American Bronx enclave during the 1977 Son of Sam killings. Against Dan Flory's reading of the film as a veiled lynching parable, he contends Lee dismantles any clean line between the psychopath Berkowitz and his supposed innocent victims: the vigilantes become victimizers, punk outsider Richie doubles the killer through his violent stage act, and Vinny destroys himself through compulsive infidelity. Evil is shown as symptomatic of a whole social order in decline rather than located in one monster.

Finnegan reads Do the Right Thing as a dramatization of philosophical skepticism and the 'problem of other minds,' using Wittgenstein's private-language argument, Austin's speech acts, and Cavell to argue that racism is not an epistemic failure to 'know' the Other but an ethical refusal to acknowledge. She shows Lee's split cinematic style (naturalistic interiority for the Italian Americans, alienating canted wide-angle shots for Radio Raheem and the black characters) enacts what being 'othered' looks like, while the Racial Slur Montage stages words as perlocutionary acts and Arendt's 'space of appearances' explains the black characters' exclusion. Mookie's thrown trash can and Sal's Wall of Fame register powerlessness rather than resolution.

Abrams's editorial introduction argues that Kubrick's whole filmography forms a coherent cinematic existentialism in which the isolated self stands against a cold, uncaring world. It threads the individual Kubrick films through named philosophers - Camus's absurd in Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove, Nietzsche's flux and Overman in Full Metal Jacket and 2001, Heidegger's thrownness and being-toward-death in Paths of Glory, Kant's marriage-morality in Eyes Wide Shut - and notes Kubrick blends this existentialism with Stoicism (The Killing) and pragmatism. It frames each contributor's essay as reading one film through that lens.

Cooke reads Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove as studies of how we face Camus's absurd. In Fear and Desire the detached Lieutenant is Camus's lucid 'stranger,' while Sidney goes mad and Mac chooses a suicidal assassination as false meaning; each faces death alone, so it is not tragedy. In Dr. Strangelove the individual is dissolved into insane institutions - Ripper, Bat Guano, the War Room round table - so no one can face the absurd lucidly; Cooke uses Sartre's bad faith to name how men become mere representatives of their institutions, and contrasts both films with Descartes's and Plato's method of certainty.

Conard argues Full Metal Jacket dramatizes Nietzsche's flux metaphysics, rooted in Heraclitus: reality is ceaseless change with no fixed 'thing,' so Sergeant Hartman's attempt to erase the recruits' individuality (shaved heads, nicknames, identical drills) is a doomed imposition of order on chaos. Private Pyle, who keeps his real name and personality, embodies that impossibility and his murder-suicide unleashes the chaotic Vietnam half. Conard links the collapse of oppositions (combatant/civilian, sacred/profane) and Nietzsche's death of God and will to power to show that in a world in flux absolutist morality fails and 'not all killings are alike' - Joker's mercy-killing of the sniper is humane where Leonard's is senseless.

Holt reads Paths of Glory as an illustration of existential ethics. The doomed men of the 701st are 'thrown' (Heidegger) into a suicidal attack on the Ant Hill, and the film contrasts the authentic Colonel Dax - sincere, consistent, refusing Mireau's command out of integrity - with the inauthentic, bad-faith General Mireau. Holt resolves the 'paradox of existentialism' by treating 'be authentic' as a formal meta-value, and argues that authenticity ultimately rests on the Aristotelian virtue of courage, shown when Paris 'dies well' before the firing squad despite an earlier failure of nerve.

Hoffman reads Eyes Wide Shut as Kubrick's most optimistic film, about whether marital fidelity can be chosen rather than accidental. Bill's confidence in his own and Alice's fidelity is a Kantian appeal - duty and rational principle over inclination - which Alice's confession of overwhelming desire for the naval officer, and Bill's night among the masked orgy, expose as vulnerable to uncontrollable desire and moral luck. Hoffman argues that by unmasking and honestly acknowledging these desires (and drawing on Kierkegaard on marriage existing 'in time') the Harfords consciously rechoose their marriage, so their fidelity is no longer merely accidental.

Decker reads Killer's Kiss (with 2001, A Clockwork Orange, and Eyes Wide Shut) to recover the philosophy of the body against the Socratic-Platonic-Cartesian denigration of the somatic. Using Merleau-Ponty's existential phenomenology ('I am my body') and pragmatists like Shusterman and Sullivan, he shows Kubrick's obsessive use of space, contingency, and the visceral - Davy's boxing match, the mannequin-warehouse fight, the weightless bodies of 2001, the Ludovico brainwashing of Alex, and the anonymous masked bodies of Eyes Wide Shut - to argue that subjectivity is corporeal and that anonymity of bodies can fund Foucauldian domination rather than liberation.

The editors' introduction surveys the volume and frames Soderbergh as a maker of 'philosophical cinema' whose films engage epistemology, metaphysics, and ethics. It previews the essays' claims: that sex, lies, and videotape and Schizopolis stage epistemological questions of truth, evidence, and skepticism; that The Underneath and The Limey use Bergson's durée to explore time and self-understanding; that Traffic tests Kant's ethics against Sartrean individual decision; and that Solaris recasts memory and authenticity via Augustine and Baudrillard's simulacra. It positions Soderbergh within Indiewood filmmaking after Welles as a self-reflexive artist.

Rodriguez-Ruiz argues that Schizopolis and sex, lies, and videotape function as everyday 'thought experiments' about knowledge, contrasting them with Descartes's evil-genius and dream arguments and Dretske's disguised-zebra case. Fletcher must literally become his wife's lover's double to know she is cheating, and Ann pieces together John's affair from a stray earring, dramatizing how high the bar for knowledge of others is and how much depends on lucky accident. The trashcan-music scene stages the problem of induction and Lehrer's Mr. Truetemp. Soderbergh's boss's 'confirm nor deny' speech and Lester's preventable death show the films endorse a moderate skepticism that still affirms nature and power as real, rejecting full relativism and dogmatism.

Tzioumakis reads sex, lies, and videotape through Lyotard's The Postmodern Condition, arguing the film is contradictory as a 'postmodern' text. Its four characters (Graham, Ann, Cynthia, John) acquire self-knowledge not from the celebrated video camera but through what Lyotard calls the flexible networks of language games: Graham's 'unexpected moves' displace Ann and Cynthia, who then master his interrogative game, while John's reactive lying dooms him. Tzioumakis contends the film's neat character transformations are legitimated by this agonistic network yet remain wedded to a strong emancipation 'master narrative' plus heterosexuality and patriarchy, undercutting its reputation as exemplary postmodern cinema and linking it back to modernity.

Pomerance combines philosophy of sex and philosophy of language to argue that sex, lies, and videotape is less about sex than about speaking sex and being watched speaking it. He analyzes Cynthia's videotaped confession about her first encounter, showing how her circumlocutions ('smooth like a test tube,' 'Ladies first') tease and withhold, and how Graham as silent 'priest of carnality' becomes an absent audience. Videotape 'amplifies' situated speech to a diffuse mass audience, so Cynthia's sexuality becomes a 'television personality,' pornographic in form and effacing her individuality in the manner of Benjamin's mechanical reproduction. The face and presence-in-time make every filmed performance both erotic and a kind of illuminating lie.

Palmer argues that The Underneath and The Limey fuse film noir's obsession with the untranscendable past with Alain Resnais's Bergsonism, mediated by Deleuze's account of the time-image. In The Limey, career criminal Wilson's consciousness accumulates recollection-images (including Poor Cow footage of a young Stamp) and prospective imaginings (the two visualized shootings), building toward a Bergsonian intuition: confronting Terry Valentine, Wilson recognizes himself as the same kind of selfish betrayer and spares him, achieving a redemption denied noir predecessors like Get Carter's Carter and Point Blank's Walker. The Underneath, by contrast, uses achronic color-coded structure only to define Michael from the outside, which Palmer counts a partial failure of the same interior ambition.

King analyzes The Limey as 'Get Carter as made by Alain Resnais,' using Bordwell's fabula/syuzhet distinction to show how its nonlinear editing renders what Soderbergh calls the nonlinear nature of thought. Dialogue continuity is stretched across discontinuous spaces (the Wilson-Elaine 'embarrassed/ashamed/disappointed' exchange), flash-forwards precede events, and the party shooting is replayed three times as Wilson's fantasy. King argues the whole film reads as Wilson's subjective reconstruction on the plane home, grounded in Bergson (via Deleuze's time-image) yet, unlike Resnais's Marienbad, never producing real ontological or epistemological doubt because the revenge-thriller backbone and color-coding keep it legible. The film's dominant note is nostalgia for a past that, because of Wilson's imprisonments, never really was.

The editor's introduction frames the whole collection around three topics in Burton's corpus—identity, authority, and aesthetics—and previews each essay. On identity it contrasts an essentialist "core self" with an empirical, experience-built self, using Big Fish and Batman Returns as test cases; on authority it surveys Mars Attacks!, Sleepy Hollow, and Batman; on aesthetics it points to Sweeney Todd, death, and color. It functions as a roadmap that argues Burton's films merit philosophical reading rather than advancing one philosopher's thesis.

Ken Hada argues that Big Fish dramatizes a narrative, intersubjective account of the self against essentialist and Cartesian views. Dying storyteller Ed Bloom builds his identity through fantastic tales (the giant catfish, the Witch), while his journalist son Will—who dismisses the stories as lies—illustrates a 'circumscribed self' that refuses the social shaping every self undergoes. Drawing on Sartre's consciousness-as-nothingness and 'the Other teaches who I am,' Mead's generalized other, Aboulafia's mediating self, and Benjamin's 'The Storyteller,' Hada reads Will's climactic act of telling his father's death-scene as his becoming a mediating storyteller and granting Ed narrative immortality. Hume's 'bundle'/self-as-fiction and Descartes' cogito are invoked as the poles Ed's storied self transcends.

Ryan Weldon reads Selina Kyle's transformation into Catwoman in Batman Returns through Sartre's existentialism and Beauvoir's The Second Sex. Pre-death Selina is Sartre's inauthentic 'waiter,' performing a servile secretary role in bad faith, and Beauvoir's objectified Other, defined by Max Shreck and the men who dismiss her. Her murder and feline resurrection free repressed drives, and her refusal of Batman's fairy-tale rescue—'I couldn't live with myself'—plus her choice to kill Shreck are cast as an assertion of facticity and transcendence, an authentic (if unfinished) self-creation that rejects the roles available to women rather than reaching a stable ending.

Daniel Sullivan argues that Burton and Poe channel childhood 'ontological insecurity' (R. D. Laing) into horror fantasy, using Burton's short Vincent as case study. Seven-year-old Vincent Malloy, imagining himself as Vincent Price, escapes 'necessity's despair' into fantastic possibility but slides into what Kierkegaard's Sickness unto Death calls defiant then demonic despair, clinging to a self-as-victim identity until he collapses. Sullivan reads fantasy as both consolation and danger—the flight into possibility further isolates the insecure child—and extends the possibility/necessity dialectic and Otto Rank's life/creation dialectic to Nightmare Before Christmas, Edward Scissorhands, and Big Fish.

Mark Walling argues that the appeal of Burton-Depp characters lies in a recovered model of childhood consciousness. Against Freud's and Piaget's view that children perceive less and are locked in the here-and-now, Walling uses Alison Gopnik's cognitive science ('babies are more conscious than we are') and Rousseau's romantic ideal of the naturally good, untutored child to read Edward Scissorhands and Ed Wood. Edward is a naturally gifted, innocent artist destroyed by a corrupt suburban 'society'; Ed Wood, megaphone in hand, is 'an eight-year-old who wants to be a movie director,' whose inattentional, make-believe joy in filmmaking—not the finished product—embodies the wide, wondering child mind Burton celebrates.

Paul A. Cantor argues that Mars Attacks! inverts the pro-government ideology of 1950s flying-saucer films (Earth vs. the Flying Saucers, Invaders from Mars, The Day the Earth Stood Still) in which scientific and military elites save a helpless public. Burton instead mocks Washington's vain, media-obsessed, multicultural establishment—Kessler, President Dale, the generals—who all fail, while Kansas 'trailer trash,' a Las Vegas boxer, and truant video-gaming kids improvise the defense; Slim Whitman's yodeling, not the state, defeats the Martians. Cantor reads the film through Tocqueville's Democracy in America on the self-organizing power of citizens' associations and the danger of soft despotism, and against Hobbes/The Day the Earth Stood Still's Leviathan solution, casting Burton as a Tocquevillian celebrant of ordinary Americans over their governing elite.

essays: Introduction War Films and the Ineffability of War
War Pictures Digital Surveillance from Foreign Theater to Homeland Security Front
Lenses into War Digital Vérité in Iraq War Films
Beyond Panopticism The Biopolitical Labor of Surveillance and War in Contemporary Film
Seeing Soldiers, Seeing Persons Wittgenstein, Film Theory, and Charlie Chaplin’s Shoulder Arms
Apocalypse Within The War Epic as Crisis of Self-Identity
The Violated Body Affective Experience and Somatic Intensity in Zero Dark Thirty
“All in War with Time” Medium as Meditation in Sherman’s March
The Power of Memory and the Memory of Power Wars and Graves in Westerns and Jidaigeki
The Ubiquitous Absence of the Enemy in Contemporary Israeli War Films
General Patton and Private Ryan The Conflicting Reality of War and Films about War
The Work of Art in the Age of Embedded Journalism Fiction versus Depiction in Zero Dark Thirty
Vernacular Metaphysics On Terrence Malick’s The Thin Red Line
War and Its Fictional Recovery On-Screen Narrative Management of Death in The Big Red One and The Thin Red Lin
“Profoundly Unreconciled to Nature” Ecstatic Truth and the Humanistic Sublime in Werner Herzog’s War Films
samples: LaRocca argues that a war film can never be war itself but only a mediated, post-facto fabrication, and reads the camera and the gun as twinned instruments ('point and shoot' becoming digital 'point and click' in Skyfall). He mobilizes Baudrillard's claim that the Gulf War 'did not take place' to describe war video games and CGI spectacle (Avatar, Call of Duty) as hyperreal simulacra, and Freud's 'Why War?' letter and death instinct to explain the compulsive proliferation of war representation. Foucault ('peace is a coded war'), Heraclitus ('war is father of all'), and Isaiah Berlin's plurality of incompatible values frame war's ineffability and perpetuity, while Cavell's ontology of film grounds the viewer's 'mechanically assured' helplessness before on-screen dying bodies.

Jameson contends that war poses the 'nominalist dilemma'—the gap between abstract totality and sensory immediacy—making it ultimately unrepresentable, and enumerates eight recurring narrative situations (existential, collective, leaders, technology, landscape, atrocity, homeland attack, occupation). Using Burke's dramatistic pentad he argues the war narrative drifts from 'act/agent' toward 'scene,' where the anthropomorphic dissolves; Sartre's 'groups-in-fusion' and Deleuze's nomadic war machine model the collective buddy-squad, whose division of labor he compares to the heist film. Reading Grimmelshausen's Simplicissimus and Döblin's Wallenstein against Kluge's Stalingrad and Halberstadt collages, he shows war (from the Thirty Years' War to WWII aerial bombing) generating a rhizomatic, nonnarrative flow that defeats stable narrative convention.

Stewart argues that War on Terror films (Redacted, Battle for Haditha, The Situation, In the Valley of Elah, Waltz with Bashir) depict 'a soldiery without a genre' because digital surveillance has fused sighting and triggering, so combat is nowhere and everywhere and the classic movement-image spectacle collapses. Drawing on Deleuze's movement-image/time-image distinction, he recasts the soldier as spectator (SSS' rather than SAS'), watching under the panoptic drone eye rather than acting, and shows sci-fi 'temportation' thrillers (Déjà Vu, Source Code, Eagle Eye) travestying the time-image into computerized wish-fulfillment. The Hurt Locker succeeds precisely by reverting to a man-vs-machine 'duel,' while Waltz with Bashir alone achieves genuine political reframing by breaking from animation into archival massacre footage.

Peebles defends the 'digital vérité' of Iraq War films (Stop-Loss, In the Valley of Elah, The Battle for Haditha, Redacted, Standard Operating Procedure) against Garrett Stewart's charge that grainy embedded footage elides critique, arguing instead that the multiplying lenses close the distance between soldier and viewer to build empathy. She invokes Baudrillard's 'the Gulf War did not take place' to show how CNN's video-game-like distance erased the common soldier, which the up-close soldier-shot cell-phone image corrects. Reading Hank Deerfield's reconstruction of his son's fatal Humvee incident in Elah and Errol Morris's reframing of the Abu Ghraib photos in Standard Operating Procedure, she argues each frame is 'both an aperture and a restriction,' and that these tragedies are inherently antiwar.

Gooch argues that the post-2005 surveillance film cycle moves 'beyond panopticism': Foucault's disciplinary gaze gives way to Deleuze's 'societies of control,' and the surveiling gaze becomes direct domination and a form of biopolitical labor (Hardt and Negri) rather than an impersonal structure. He reads the prestige dramas (Redacted, Stop-Loss, In the Valley of Elah, Lions for Lambs) as exposing the soldier's proletarianization and self-surveillance, and the thrillers/blockbusters (Déjà Vu, The Kingdom, Body of Lies, The Bourne Ultimatum, Eagle Eye, Burn after Reading) as staging a Marxist antagonism between living labor (the watching hero) and the fixed capital of surveillance technology. Using Deleuze's 'degraded time-image,' Kant's needed separation of subject and law, and Benjamin/Agamben's state of exception, he shows Eagle Eye inverting law and subject to justify preemptive war and turn biopolitical labor into the labor of subjection.

Hilsabeck argues that Wittgenstein's notion of aspect perception ("seeing as") is not a phenomenology of illusion, as film theorists like Allen and Turvey take it, but an ethical matter of articulating experience within forms of life and language games. He reads Chaplin's Shoulder Arms through this lens: Doughboy's tree-disguise gag and his repurposing of war objects (Limburger cheese as grenade, gramophone horn as snorkel) demonstrate imaginative, ethical vision, while the German soldier who cannot see the tree-as-man exhibits "aspect blindness." The film makes viewers' willingness to "see anew" a test of attunement and mutual acknowledgment, casting the environment of WWI trench warfare and mechanized shock as what stifles this imaginative seeing.

samples: McMahon and Csaki's introduction argues that the western and philosophy are joined through the mimetic theory of art (the western as a mirror of frontier history) and through shared interest in identity, community, and morality. It frames the volume's four parts and previews each essay, noting that canonical western tropes trace back to Plato and Aristotle and that films like High Noon, Shane, and The Searchers dramatize abstract philosophical theories. It treats the western as an unexplored 'frontier' for philosophic analysis rather than defending one thesis of its own.

Biderman argues that the western hero's solitude carries philosophical benefits, distinguishing being alone from feeling lonely (McCauley in Heat: 'I'm alone, I'm not lonely'). Epistemically he likens the silent, self-reliant hero (Kane in High Noon, Shane, Munny in Unforgiven, Blondie) to Descartes retreating into methodological doubt and solipsistic solitude to secure knowledge. Ethically he sets Aristotle's claim that man is a social animal (so the friendless hero cannot flourish) against Stoic detachment and Sartrean/existentialist authenticity, concluding the hero must be 'lone' because his heroism is inseparable from his chosen solitude.

Den Uyl builds a composite philosophic picture of self-sufficiency from Aristotle's autarkeia (reason-guided virtuous activity, requiring external goods and civilization) and Spinoza's freedom as acting from one's own nature guided by adequate ideas, then tests it on John Ford's heroes. In The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance, Tom Doniphon is 'procedurally' self-sufficient in the precivilized West while Ransom Stoddard embodies civilized reason, and neither can inhabit the other's world. He argues the western's deepest value is Emersonian self-reliance—fidelity to one's own unique nature (the 'cactus rose')—which civilization threatens even as it enables Aristotelian flourishing.

Csaki argues that John Wayne became the ultimate cinematic cowboy because his characters embody classical American pragmatism. Using William James's squirrel-and-tree parable and Dewey's account of 'inquiry' transforming an indeterminate situation, he reads Rooster Cogburn's split-second raft decision and Wil Anderson's hiring of schoolboys in The Cowboys as pragmatic problem-solving from experience. He treats the 'code of the West' not as fixed absolutes but as rules applied pragmatically (Rooster shooting men in the back, the cowboys letting Long Hair be dragged to death), where truth is what can be assimilated, verified, and made to 'work.'

Mexal reads both versions of 3:10 to Yuma through Locke's classical liberalism, arguing the western hero descends from Locke's autonomous, property-owning self in a 'state of nature' (contrasted with Hobbes's state of war). In the 1957 film, Dan Evans transforms from atomistic self-interest to a masculine civic republicanism, escorting Ben Wade to the train even after being released from his contract, reflecting Cold War anxieties. In the 2007 remake, Dan instead renegotiates his contract for water rights and money, so western masculinity becomes unyielding Lockean individualism and the 'right to get rich' in a post-Cold War, capitalist-triumphant America.

Collins analyzes the railroad in Tycoon and both versions of 3:10 to Yuma, drawing on feminist critics (Irigaray, Bordo, Grosz, Haraway, Merchant) who expose a masculinist 'panoramic' epistemology coding mind as male and passive nature/landscape as female. She argues trains destabilize rather than confirm this mastery: in Tycoon, Johnny Munroe conflates conquering the feminized Andean landscape with dominating his wife Maura, yet the bridge and train fail; in the 2007 Yuma, the railroad's promise of masculine legitimacy is sustained only by 'cruel optimism' and male homosocial love between Dan Evans and Ben Wade, over anxieties about racial Others (Apache, Chinese laborers).

samples: Kowalski's editorial introduction previews all three sections of the volume, framing the collection around the idea that philosophy is something one 'does' and that Spielberg's films (from Jaws to A.I., Schindler's List, Amistad, Munich, and Minority Report) raise questions in ethics, aesthetics, mind, and political philosophy. It names each contributor's thesis rather than arguing an original one, and closes by posing the meta-question of whether popular film can itself 'do' philosophy.

Arms and Riley argue that Spielberg fuses spectacle with intimate 'broken family' drama, then use War of the Worlds, A.I., and Empire of the Sun to press the philosophical problem of special (agent-relative) obligations. They show that Ray's redemption (even murdering Ogilvy to protect Rachel), Gigolo Joe's protection of David, and John Graham's failure all turn on duties to the innocent that consequentialism's agent-neutral, greatest-good calculus cannot accommodate, formalizing the clash as a valid argument against consequentialism. They suggest Spielberg grounds these special obligations in the intrinsic worth of 'the Innocent.'

Le Gall and Taliaferro read E.T., Hook, and the Indiana Jones trilogy through a Socratic-Platonic ideal in which the true 'adventure' ends not in glory (kleos) but in homecoming, beauty, and restored parent-child love. Indiana abandons the grail to grab his father's hand and hears 'Indiana' instead of 'Junior'; Elliott becomes a father to E.T. while E.T. teaches him loss; Peter Banning must recover his Pan-childhood to save his kids. They tie this to the Republic's Myth of Er, the Symposium's ladder of love, and xenia (hospitality) as the setting for wisdom.

Wright argues that Spielberg's cinematic language (shot scale, montage editing, mise-en-scene) enacts Levinas's ethics of alterity, in which meeting the unknowable 'face' of the Other demands responsibility and sacrifice, wisdom through love rather than knowledge. He contrasts the distancing long shots that render the Jaws shark and The Thing as mere threats with the intimate close-ups that 'reveal the face' in Close Encounters and E.T., then shows Schindler's List turning the same technique onto the human Other, using the red coat as the face that pulls Schindler from detachment into responsibility.

Trogan and Kowalski use Jaws to pose the paradox of fiction: we feel real fear and pity for Chrissie, the Kintners, and Quint though we know they are not real. They rehearse Radford's charge that such emotions are incoherent (since based on false belief) and answer it with a cognitivist 'unasserted thought' account and Kendall Walton's theory of make-believe, arguing we self-consciously enter the film as an adult game. Drawing on Nussbaum, they claim appropriate emotional response to Jaws cultivates empathy and 'seeing,' honing ethical sensitivity rather than turning adults into children.

Dunn interprets A.I. as a meditation on the 'tragic sense of life': treating David as a person, he argues the film dramatizes three doomed human desires (love, uniqueness, immortality) and tests two failed escapes from mortality, science (Professor Hobby, the Flesh Fair, David's suicide leap) and religious faith (the fraudulent Blue Fairy at drowned Coney Island). Defending the maligned finale, he reads the simulated Blue Fairy and the one-day resurrection of Monica as raising whether a perfect simulation of love can be 'real enough,' with David achieving a sober humanistic acceptance of impermanence.
